chunks.content: Hopefully at this point, I’ve made the compelling case for why there are more buyers and more sellers of small businesses than ever before. You wouldn’t be surprised to learn that along with this flood of interest has come a series of social media gurus. guru, some are absolute sages and some are charlatans. Folks can get rich relatively quickly selling each other on the clickbait dream of buying a ‘boring business’ and running it remotely from your sailboat in the mediterranean. That’s not real. While I I do to get my own advice from people who didn’t make their millions selling books about how to make millions. Moreover, the gurus often have a book that promises to tell you how to choose a business to buy, how to run your own proprietary search, how to secure financing for the business, how to conduct the transaction to acquire that business, how to transition that business into your new ownership, and how to improve the operations of that business. Here’s my hot take: that is entirely too many things for a single book to cover. Gurus are leading masterminds filled with packs of buyers and they’re serving a valuable role of educators in this space, but unfortunately the gurus themselves often have relatively limited experience in acquiring. Because they’re speaking to a wide audience with varying levels of experience, and they’re trying to package complex processes into digestible sound bites. Content creation, running masterminds, hosting webinars, managing an online presence—it’s a business in and of itself. So when someone’s out there posting twice a day about how to run an HVAC company, you can be sure they’re not fixing broken compressors or managing dispatch. Who has the time? And , no shade—building an audience is hard worktrust me, I’m actively trying! But let’s not confuse that with operating experience. There's a difference between running a business and running a personal brand. Just because someone bought a car wash once doesn’t make them a seasoned operator. But in the Instagram era, it’s not that hard to throw on a backward cap, record a reel in your Tesla, and suddenly you're an “acquisition expert.” Building and scaling content-driven influence requires a different set of muscles than operating a small business. They’re not out there managing teams, solving cash flow problems, or juggling client crises—they’re optimizing their email funnels and shooting YouTube videos. That doesn’t mean what they’re teaching has zero value, but it does mean we need to contextualize it. If someone’s entire livelihood comes from teaching acquisitions rather than doing them, there’s a ceiling on how deep their insights can go. I’m not a guru (yet, but please like and subscribe so I can finally relax). I’m just a dumb lawyer. I’ve built a legal practice that I love and a consulting company that, while deeply fulfilling, both spit off a sometimes annoyingly great living—but neither has any real enterprise value. They’re not sellable. If I stop showing up, they stop working. Same with my niche Airbnb side hustle and my tiny sliver of equity in other people’s . But in my dumb lawyer role, sitting on the sidelines of deals every day, I see it happen—over and over. Buyers feeling their way through a confusing process, stepping into the same potholes I could’ve told them were coming. Or Rachel, a smart, capable buyer who had the money and the motivation but assumed she’d be “guided” through the transaction by the seller’s broker. She didn’t realize the broker was barely playing traffic cop, and nobody told her about quality of earnings, transition planning, or the 7216 consent forms her seller was going to demand she obtain. It was like watching someone try to fly a plane by reading a travel blog. Then there’s Tom and Lisa, seller and buyer who liked each other—a lot. Great alignment, same values, even shared a love of spreadsheets (no, seriously). But they kept brushing off the messy stuff and avoiding the hard discussions. Tom didn’t want to talk about client attrition he had been experiencing, and Lisa assumed she could fix operations post-close. They closed without digging in. Six months later? Lisa’s realizing how understaffed Tom had been and she is buried in backlogged extensions eanwhile Tom’s note isn’t getting timely paid and he hasn’t yet spent a single day on the golf course. So—I can’t not try to educate people. I’m a professional who sees behind the curtain often enough to know where the trapdoors are.

A former partner, a longtime employee, a peer from your referral network. These were people who understood your business, your clients, your quirks, and your value. You didn’t need to educate them on what busy season feels like or why your billing system is the way it is. The relationship helped carry the deal forward, smoothing over bumps that might otherwise become big issues. And when something unexpected came up? Sell to a Stranger (And the Game Has Changed) Historically, selling to a stranger meant . Private equity firms or large consolidators with full M&A departments would run the show. They had checklists, teams, lawyers, and systems—and while you might not have loved the power dynamic, at least there was a process. You knew where the train was going, even if you weren’t the one driving it. That’s not always the case anymore. Today, more “strangers” are individual buyers—search funders, first-time entrepreneurs, or people new to accounting altogether. They don’t have a playbook. They’re not showing up with a ready-made process to guide the deal forward. And if you're the seller, you often can’t run the process yourself either—not effectively—because it’s simply not your job, and you’re trying to run the business (while keeping it profitable and growing to boot). More Sellers. But Still No Infrastructure Here’s the paradox: the market for small business deals is exploding. More business owners are retiring than ever before. More buyers are entering the space—thanks to search funds, solo capitalists, and first-time acquirers. Yet the infrastructure to support these deals is nowhere near where it needs to be. This isn’t just inefficient—it’s dangerous. Deals fall apart, or worse, close with terms that create landmines for both sides down the road. People go bankrupt, lives are destroyed, legacies are lost as business owners, exasperated, throw their businesses away after a deal falls through. I’m not being overly dramatic here; I see it every day. BOX A note from experience: Years ago, after I left Big Law, I tried applying my upper-middle-market training to small deals. It... didn’t go well. The documents were overkill, the parties were confused, and the clients weren’t thrilled to hear that they'd need to loop in a tax lawyer, real estate lawyer, employment lawyer—build their own legal Avengers team to get through a basic transaction. The deal studies I relied on were steering me in the wrong direction, and the brokers and bankers? I was increasingly getting the feeling that they liked me, but didn’t LOVE me.... Eventually, I scrapped the Big Law playbook entirely. These days, I meet a lot of sharp, Wall Street-type buyers—folks who’ve been running acquisitions for funds or managing portfolios for years and now want to build their own wealth. They’re ready to apply what they’ve learned. And I give them the same advice I had to learn the hard way: Don’t distill down from the upper market—build up from common sense. Instead of taking a 100-page contract and trying to chop it down to fit, start fresh. Write the deal in plain language that makes sense for what you're buying. Add complexity only where the deal calls for it. That way, your contract reflects the business you’re buying—not some abstract template from a billion-dollar transaction. A System Built for Big Deals, Not Small Ones The legal side doesn’t make it easier. The current deal process was built for large transactions—ones that justify $100,000+ in legal fees. Lawyers on both sides go back and forth, often more concerned with planting gotchas in the documents than simplifying or clarifying the deal. But for a small acquisition—say $1 million to $5 million—this system breaks down: Good M&A law firms don’t touch these deals. Founders can’t afford six-figure legal bills. The lawyers who are available may not have the M&A experience needed to protect their client in a sophisticated deal. And unlike residential real estate—which has standardized forms, clear regulations, and state-level oversight—small business M&A has no unified system. There’s no governing body. No standard forms. Broker regulation is patchy at best, varying state by state. Some join the IBBA (International Business Brokers Association), but it’s voluntary, and the enforcement power is minimal. So What Happens? What happens is this: you have two parties—often both first-timers—navigating a process that was never designed for them. One is trying to exit something they built over decades. The other is trying to step into ownership for the first time. Both are making one of the biggest financial and career-defining decisions of their lives, and yet... they’re doing it with minimal support, limited experience, and no clear roadmap. The traditional M&A system assumes someone at the table knows what they’re doing. That there’s a full-time deal team. That one party—usually the buyer—has done this before and is driving the process with discipline and skill. But when that’s not the case? When neither party is a seasoned dealmaker? The entire process becomes shaky, inefficient, and vulnerable to collapse. There’s no playbook. No standard forms. No agreed-upon flow. Everyone is guessing. Everyone is Googling. Everyone is relying on advice from brokers who may or may not have any training, or lawyers who are trying to apply big-deal strategies to a $1.5M practice sale. And when the cost of doing it the “right” way—hiring a top M&A attorney, a CPA to do a QofE, an industry consultant, and a lending specialist—is looking pretty to the deal’s purchase price?

A booming market of small business transactions... with no infrastructure, no affordability, and no standardization. And that’s exactly why we need a new approach. Where This Is Going This book is hoping to provide some insight to people looking to run a deal and get them over their Dunning Kruger hump so they can more thoughtfully project-manage their deal. So many clients come to me, hat in hand, saying ‘I don’t know, what I don’t know.’ I want this book to teach you what you don’t know! But, despite my efforts with DealAcademy.Org and all the relentless content all of us are pushing out on the internet, sometimes the more realistic goal (and certainly the more common result) is that the clients learn what they don’t know and can more intentionally focus limited resources to bolster the gaps. I also advocate for changes to the system. We need to standardize these documents, the diligence process, and align parties’ expectations. We need more thoughtful, ethical, and experienced parties and intermediaries to support this process. We need to expand what we require of our brokers. (Note I know I’m being hard on brokers here, but there are really awesome ones, just find me and ask!) It’s time for a smarter model. Because for most of us, this isn’t a transaction—it’s the defining transaction of their lives. THE SMALL BUSINESS BUYING ECOSYSTEM 1. Investment Bankers vs. Brokers n the upper market, you’ll find the classic investment bankers—the ones with skyline views, tailored suits, and packed calendars. They’re staying late, waking up early, and living off caffeine and closing calls. Basically, they are the living embodiment of that cheesy stock photo labeled “Businessperson.” Total aside, but stay with me—remember the movie Hook? Robin Williams plays a grown-up Peter Pan who’s forgotten his magical past and rebranded as a... investment banker. In one of the opening scenes, he misses his kid’s baseball game because he’s on a brick-sized cell phone trying to close a deal. That’s the cultural image we all have burned into our heads: the stressed, slick, always-on deal guy. That’s what “broker” looks like in our collective imagination. One thing that changes the environment in small business buying is the lack of investment bankers AND the presence of business brokers. Investment bankers and business brokers are not the same thing—even though they both help people buy and sell businesses, and both are very good at what they do. But the way they do it? Different planets. The Paycheck Breakdown Let’s start with the obvious: they get paid differently. Business brokers typically focus on smaller, Main Street to lower middle-market businesses (think $500K to $5M in revenue), and they’re usually compensated on a commission-only basis—around % of the sale price is standard. That sounds like a lot, but they’re often the ones doing all the heavy lifting: valuation, marketing, buyer screening, and navigating the emotional rollercoaster that is a business sale. They're part advisor, part therapist, part negotiator. Solid generalist professionals who know how to get a deal across the finish line. Investment bankers, on the other hand, usually work on larger, more complex deals. Their fee structures tend to include a retainer plus a success fee, often in the 1–3% range, depending on deal size (the bigger the deal, the smaller the percentage). Their work usually kicks in when there’s a need for strategic positioning, institutional buyers, layered financing, or private equity—think deals over $20M, often much more. Credentials and Regs: It’s a Whole Thing Now here’s where it really splits. Investment bankers are highly regulated—we’re talking FINRA licenses, SEC compliance, and all the acronyms that make most people’s eyes glaze over. Most have Wall Street training or MBAs, and they live in the land of fairness opinions, CIMs (confidential information memorand), and data rooms. They’re required to be licensed to sell securities, which often comes into play with more complex business sales or capital raises. Brokers, on the other hand, generally aren’t subject to the same federal regulations. In many states, they might be required to hold a real estate license. They’re usually more sales-focused, working one-on-one with business owners, and they often know the local market inside and out. Many are former business owners themselves—which can be a huge asset when guiding clients through their first-ever sale. Some have remarkably backgrounds spanning all kinds of industries where they bought and sold businesses in multiple different capacities and some have almost no business experience or training. When the big leagues coming down to the small business world, the parties are quite simply not speaking the same language. When I first began gaining traction in the small business M&A space, I’ll admit—I carried a bit of a chip on my shoulder when it came to business brokers. Part of that came from seeing the settlement statements at closing—the final documents that show where all the money is wired. It’s hard not to stare when you see 10% (or more) of the purchase price going out as a broker fee. That number looks a whole lot different when it’s in six figures and staring back at you in bold. What really caught me off guard, though, was how often I had no idea there was even a broker involved. I’d been on daily calls with buyers and sellers for months, helping push the deal forward, navigating the emotional highs and lows, solving problems—and then out of nowhere, I’d see a previously unnamed party getting a major payout. It was a bit of a gut-check moment. Who were they? What role did they play? Over time, my perspective has evolved. While those early experiences raised questions, I’ve come to understand that brokers operate in a different lane. They may not always be in the weeds of every negotiation, but they often play a role at the front end—finding the buyer, framing the opportunity, and moving the process forward in ways that aren't always visible post-LOI. And in many deals, especially with first-time sellers, having someone who understands both the emotional and financial side of the transition can be helpful. Only about 20% of small business deals are brokered, leaving 80% to be transacted in the wild. For this reason—and plenty of others—there’s been a growing chorus in recent years around the idea of bypassing the broker altogether. In the buyer community, especially among private equity groups and search funds, this has become a full-fledged strategy known as “proprietary outreach.” In plain terms, it means buyers are proactively scouring the internet, industry directories, LinkedIn, and local business sites to find business owners who may be quietly open to selling, but haven’t formally listed their company with a broker.

At least in my experience, the risk of failure is significantly higher when there’s no broker. Here’s one big reason: owning a business isn’t a job—it’s an identity. It’s the frame through which many people have lived their lives for decades. Asking someone to go from running a company full-time to walking away—financially, emotionally, and operationally—in 45 to 60 days is a tall order. And often, in the early stages of a deal, sellers haven't truly done the math. They might not yet know what they need at closing to feel comfortable stepping away. Sometimes they haven’t seriously considered what retirement even looks like, or how they’ll feel without the rhythms and responsibilities of business ownership. More than once, I’ve seen deals unravel midway because the seller realizes—sometimes too late—that they’re not ready for the seismic life shift. They may get to due diligence and suddenly decide the price isn’t high enough, or that they’re not sure what they’ll do next. That kind of uncertainty is tough for buyers who are already investing time, money, and resources into the process. This is where brokers quietly shine. By the time a deal hits the market with a reputable broker involved, it usually means the seller has at least begun to process the emotional and logistical aspects of exiting. They’ve been asked the hard questions. They've done some internal work. And while a broker can’t prevent cold feet entirely, they drastically reduce the chances of getting blindsided by a seller backing out late in the game. There’s a reason every broker’s lead magnet is some version of “Find out what your business is worth!”—because people always click on it. That valuation carrot is irresistible. But if a buyer finds a seller “in the wild,” they have to figure out if the business owner is serious—or fishing for an ego boost or a free valuation. Sure, some buyers are willing to kiss a bunch of frogs if it means finding that one seller who’s clueless about the market and willing to offer great terms (plus save 10% in broker fees). But that strategy comes with a cost—more wasted time, more broken deals, and higher diligence expenses. So no, it’s not as simple as saying brokered = bad and off-market = good. They don't want to make a mistake for which they will be blamed—or sued for malpractice—at a later date. How can you win with such people at the table?” Here’s the structural problem no one talks about: M&A law is a niche specialty that mostly lives inside big firms—the kind with $1,000/hour rates, an army of associates, and entire floors dedicated to high-dollar deals. That’s where most of the legal training happens, and it shows. The skillset is strong, but so is the overhead. If you’re doing a $5 million deal? You’re not a priority. You’re background noise next to the $200 million transactions they’re really focused on. And frankly, no one slows a deal down like a Big Law associate trying to justify their existence, rewriting every sentence, and “circling back” on stuff that doesn’t matter.

So what happens next? Buyers (and sellers) swing too far the other way. They hire a generalist. Someone who mostly does divorces, dabbles in injury claims, and “takes a quick look” at contracts now and then. Nice person. Smart as can be. BOX Inaction is a natural human response to uncertainty and if you give a someone a task they don’t already understand like the back of their hand, they will take 10x as long to get around to reviewing it. The problem with that is, small deals—especially in the sub-$5M range—run on momentum. They are delicate, fragile little ecosystems. It’s adjacent, it’s essential, and sometimes it even feels like business advice—but it’s not the same thing. And if you treat it like it is, you’re going to end up with a perfectly drafted, legally airtight deal that died before it could close. Here’s why: lawyers are in the business of identifying, explaining, and minimizing risk. That’s their job. And they’re usually very good at it. You want your lawyer to think about what could go wrong, to flag the loopholes, to tighten the reps and warranties, and to make sure you’re not signing something that leaves you personally liable for someone else’s bad bookkeeping from 2009. They’re not built to decide whether a deal is “worth it.” That’s your job. The Lawyer’s Lens: Risk. Risk. More Risk. To a lawyer, a “good deal” is one where every contingency is covered, every term is defined, and every liability is fully disclosed, capped, and indemnified. Their ideal version of due diligence ends in a 72-page risk memo and a flowchart that makes your eyes glaze over. That doesn’t mean they’re wrong. It means they’re looking at the deal from a completely different altitude. And they should be! That’s the job. Instead, you want folks at the bank who will advocate for you. Who will workshop a structure with you early on. Who will say, “This part is weak—can we get the seller to tweak it?” or “Here’s how we could bridge that collateral gap.” That kind of banker is worth their weight in gold. Why You Absolutely Want an SBA Preferred Lender If you’re planning to use SBA financing—and for many small business acquisitions, it’s the most accessible capital on the table—you need to work with an SBA Preferred Lender. Full stop. Why? Because not all banks are created equal under the SBA program. A Preferred Lender has earned the ability to process, approve, and close loans entirely in-house. That means no waiting for the SBA to sign off, no outside review delays, and no guesswork. They’ve got the authority to move quickly—and that’s a massive advantage in a deal environment where timing matters. Now contrast that with a non-preferred lender. They have to package up your deal and send it off to the SBA for final approval. You wait. They wait. And sometimes you get a surprise “no” weeks down the line, when you’ve already spent money on diligence and legal. That’s not a timeline you want to bet your deal on. Industry Experience Matters, Too Beyond preferred status, you want a banker—or a bank—that has actual experience financing deals in your industry. That’s especially true for professional services like accounting or financial advisory firms, which can confuse generalist lenders. A banker familiar with professional services knows how to evaluate recurring contracts, seasonality, and discretionary, knows the staffing models, and probably won’t freak out when they see owner comp baked into SDE. A banker who doesn’t know your space? They might try to apply a restaurant or retail underwriting lens to your deal—and that can send things sideways fast. Remember, you’re not borrowing money. You’re building a relationship with a financial institution that has to understand what you're buying to say yes, and say it efficiently. What About Bank Brokers? Now let’s talk about bank brokers—these are folks who act as matchmakers between you and a lender. They usually take a small percentage of the loan proceeds, and yes, a lot of them refer to the same handful of banks over and over again. That can feel a little cookie-cutter, but don’t write them off entirely. Here’s where they can be very valuable: Translation and Packaging: A good bank broker knows what the bank wants to see—and how they want to see it. They can help you package your deal in a way that maximizes your odds of approval. Think of it like applying to college with someone who used to sit on the admissions committee. Access: They often have existing relationships with specific BDOs or underwriters. That means when they say, “This is a strong deal,” the bank is more likely to listen. Heavy Lifting: If you don’t have a bank broker, you are the one pulling together all the seller’s financials, organizing them, and explaining them to the bank. A bank broker can do some of that work for you—and they’re often better at chasing down documents from a seller than you are, because that’s literally their job. That said, not all bank brokers are created equal. Some are hands-off and drop your deal like a referral code. Others are actively involved, shoulder-to-shoulder with you through the entire financing process. If you’re going to work with a bank broker, ask how engaged they’ll be, and whether they’ll help with packaging, underwriting calls, and follow-ups. Let’s go. 1-Managing Deal Fatigue Embarking on an acquisition—especially in the small to mid-sized space—isn’t only a business transaction; it’s a mental, emotional, and logistical endurance sport. It starts with a burst of excitement—kind of like the first mile of a marathon when you believe you're a runner. But as negotiations drag on, timelines stretch, and your inbox fills with follow-ups marked "URGENT" from people you’ve never heard of, reality kicks in. Welcome to the long, sweaty middle miles. Understanding Deal Fatigue and Its Implications Here’s the thing nobody tells you until you’re in it: getting a deal across the finish line is another full-time job. And unfortunately, most people already have one. The seller is running their business—keeping clients happy, managing staff, keeping the lights on. The buyer might be juggling diligence and financial modeling while working a full-time W-2 job, fielding banker calls during their lunch break and reviewing legal docs at midnight. No one’s sleeping. Everyone’s over it. And that’s when deal fatigue sets in. Deal fatigue isn’t “we’re getting tired.” It’s more like an emotional version of running out of gas in the middle of nowhere—with no cell reception and a hungry raccoon staring at you. In mergers and acquisitions (M&A), deal fatigue shows up as disengagement, missed deadlines, abrupt radio silence, or tense Zooms where someone says “per my last email” with a little too much heat. It’s the feeling that you’ve been “close” to signing for weeks—but nothing’s moving (except the projected closing date). Deal fatigue tends to track closely with how long the process drags on. The more time that passes without a clear, focused path to closing, the more likely it is that one or both sides start to lose steam. Energy fades. Enthusiasm cools. And the deal starts to wobble. Put simply: the longer it takes, the shakier it gets. 2. The Finite Nature of Deal Stamina Most sellers of sub-$5M businesses don’t have a team of advisors and analysts backing them up—they’re doing it themselves while also running their business. Same for buyers. One minute they’re prepping a diligence request list, the next they’re troubleshooting payroll software. There’s no bandwidth fairy coming to save anyone. That’s why deal stamina—your capacity to keep making thoughtful, engaged decisions—is finite. It’s a real, measurable resource, like money or calories. And once it’s gone? You’re at the mercy of stress, shortcuts, and worst of all, bad assumptions. If you’ve ever tried to negotiate while sleep-deprived, hangry, or at the end of a long week, you know how quickly good intentions can unravel. When both parties are depleted, what used to be a reasonable question (“Can we clarify this working capital adjustment?”) starts sounding like an attack. It’s a recipe for retrading, resentment, or worse, walking away. 3. Each generation brings its own set of expectations, communication styles, and deal-breaking triggers to the table. If you’re not paying attention, those subtle misalignments can turn into full-blown deal fatigue. The Unspoken Bias You Should Always Expect (and Work Around) Here’s a hard truth that’s part joke, part survival tip: older business owners often think younger business owners are lazy. Is it true? Not really...but maybe. Is it a wildly unfair overgeneralization? Absolutely. But is it something you should keep in mind if you’re the younger party in a deal? Without question. This perception isn’t about facts—it’s about feelings. And in deals, feelings move faster than facts. Maybe they see your flexible schedule and assume you’re not serious. The business had 80% of its revenue recurring and ran like a well-oiled machine. But old mental models die hard. So what do you do with that? You over-communicate your seriousness. You don’t get defensive. You show up buttoned-up, prepared, and with a plan. They came from two people sitting down, having a real conversation, and solving problems like grown-ups who trust each other. Here’s one of my all-time favorites: Donna and Jeff: A Collaborative Win-Win Donna and Jeff had been circling each other for years. Not romantically—professionally. She wasn’t going to gut the company he’d spent 25 years building. So he offered her a deal—entirely seller financed—with terms that frankly looked more generous than you'd expect for that size and quality of business. Donna was interested, but nervous. But turning it into a good deal—that comes from the work you do after you find it. The diligence you dig into. The relationships you build. The structure you negotiate. The risks you manage. I’ve seen buyers walk away from great businesses because the headline number felt too high—without ever doing the work to see how terms could shift the economics. And I’ve seen average businesses become great buys because the buyer knew how to shape the deal to fit their needs and protect their downside. The best deals are rarely perfect when you first spot them. They become great through careful planning, creative structuring, and smart negotiation. So don’t wait around for the unicorn. Learn how to build one. You don’t stumble into a good deal like you find a twenty-dollar bill in your coat pocket. You build one. Piece by piece. With strategy, care, and—believe it or not—empathy. And not any empathy. We’re talking about calculated empathy. This isn’t about being soft or sentimental. It’s about being smart enough to understand what the seller cares about, and using that insight to create alignment, craft better terms, and ultimately get to a deal that works for both sides. Because here’s the thing: you can’t tell whether a business is a “good deal” by looking at a listing. A listing shows you the shell—gross revenue, location, headcount. That’s like picking a spouse based on height and hair color. What makes a deal “good” is the intersection of the business’s features, the terms of the offer, and the emotional and strategic fit between buyer and seller. Which brings me to my grandmother, Irene. She lived to be 97.5 years old—and yes, the half-year mattered. “After 90,” she’d say, “you start counting like you're a toddler again.” She also had a phrase she loved, and it’s been lodged in my brain ever since: “There’s a lid for every pot.” She wasn’t just talking about dating (though she was also definitely talking about dating). She meant that every person, and every situation, has a complementary match—if you’re patient enough to find it. That’s what calculated empathy is in the world of business acquisitions: the practice of finding the fit, not just the numbers. What Does the Seller Care About? Spoiler: it’s rarely just the money. Yes, sellers want to get paid. Of course they do. But very few walk away from a business they’ve built with their own two hands thinking, “Hope the check clears, peace out forever.” They care about what happens next—to their team, to their clients, to their legacy. They care about whether you’ll treat the business with respect. Whether you’ll change the software their team has finally gotten used to. Whether Karen at the front desk, who brought them soup during their divorce, still has a job. Your job as the buyer is to pay attention. Listen for the subtext. Ask the second question. If the seller keeps telling you how long their bookkeeper has been with them, that’s a flag. Not a red one—a gold one. That’s someone who matters. Your deal should reflect that. If they mention they go to lunch every Friday with their original client from 1987, ask if they want to keep that client relationship going post-close as a carveout to the non-compete. These are the details that don’t make it into CIMs or spreadsheets—but they’re what the seller’s heart is anchored to. Simple enough, right? But—surprise—those two goals are the foundation. Sellers almost always have specific, personal, often quirky deal terms they care deeply about. All they wanted post-sale was to swing by once a week, chat with staff, and walk out with a muffin. No cash involved—just ritual and closure. “You can have the aquarium, but I keep the fish.” This one made sense once you knew the fish had names and the seller had raised them from tiny little pet-store fry. Again, emotional legacy. “You must rent the office space from me for the next seven years.” The seller owned the real estate. Keeping a stable tenant (a.k.a. the buyer) was part of their retirement income plan. Not optional. Non-negotiable. “You must buy the commercial property as part of the business deal.” No leasing allowed. Seller didn’t want to play landlord. They wanted a clean break, and that meant selling the business and the building in one transaction. “I need to keep access to a private office to store my watercolor paintings.” Yes, the business was being sold. But that office? That was the seller’s creative sanctuary. They wanted to keep using it a few days a week to paint, quietly and peacefully. And they asked for it. “I want to keep using the firm’s tax software to file my returns...forever.” Not for clients. Just for themselves. Free lifetime tax prep tools as a retirement perk. “You can’t change the software the team uses.” The seller was fiercely protective of their staff. They didn’t want the buyer to come in and throw everyone into a new system—especially not in month one. For them, this was about respecting the culture they’d built. And that you see the whole picture, not the P&L. A well-crafted LOI that speaks to their specific concerns—however odd, sentimental, or minor they may seem to you—sends a powerful message: “I’m not just blasting this out to 30 people. I’m writing this for you.” It builds trust. It builds momentum. And sometimes, a thoughtful, human-centered LOI with a slightly lower purchase price will beat out a cold, generic offer at full price. It’s letting someone keep their fish. Empathy as Leverage This isn’t about being manipulative. It’s about being strategically human. Her office, located in a beautiful brick building adorned with gas lamps, exuded the charm and elegance that Charleston was known for. Tom was a bright and ambitious young wealth advisor who had joined the firm fresh out of college and quickly proved himself to be an invaluable asset. From the moment Tom walked through the doors of Bright & Co., Evelyn saw a spark in him. He was eager to learn, dedicated, and shared Evelyn's vision for the firm. Tom looked at her, a mixture of surprise and excitement in his eyes. "Evelyn, are you sure? The firm won't be the same without you." Evelyn smiled warmly. One of the biggest tactical mistakes I see in negotiations—especially from first-time buyers—is trying to resolve each term one by one like it’s a checklist at a hardware store. Don’t do that. In complex negotiations, you should not lock in each miniature term in isolation. Instead, leave them all on the table until they can be resolved as a cohesive package, and then take them off together, all at once. This approach—called “package bargaining” in negotiation theory—gives you flexibility to make trade-offs that get the deal done. Maybe you give a little on the seller note, but you get shorter consulting obligations. If you resolve terms too early, you lose leverage, because you’re shrinking your deal toolkit before you know which tools you'll need. Harvard’s Program on Negotiation has long advocated for multi-issue negotiation strategies, noting that “negotiators who consider issues simultaneously, rather than sequentially, are more likely to reach win-win outcomes”—and a 2021 MIT Sloan study confirmed that package negotiators were 26% more likely to close deals than their piecemeal counterparts. Translation? Keep all the terms live until the deal comes together like a final puzzle snap. Otherwise, you’ll spend all your leverage solving for the corners, and have nothing left to finish the picture. You can’t look at each piece of the transaction—price, structure, seller financing, employment agreement, lease terms—as if they’re isolated Lego blocks. They’re more like a plate of spaghetti. Tug on one noodle, and the whole thing shifts. That’s why I’m constantly coaching buyers and sellers to resolve as many terms as possible at once. Because if you don’t? You end up in a never-ending game of term-by-term Whack-A-Mole. Raise the seller-financed amount? The seller now wants more post-close involvement. Lower the seller note interest rate? Suddenly they want more salary. They push for a quick close? You ask for a longer transition window. On and on it goes. Why Package Bargaining Is a LOI Power Play (And Why You Lose That Power After It’s Signed) The annoying part about package bargaining is you only really get to do it before the LOI is signed. After that? You're no longer building a deal—you’re coloring inside the lines of one. Here’s why. The LOI Locks In the Frame—Even When It’s "Non-Binding" Everyone loves to say that LOIs are “non-binding,” and legally, sure—that’s true. But functionally? Once both sides sign that letter, it sets the tone, structure, and framework for the rest of the deal. It becomes the working contract, even if it’s not enforceable in court. People get emotionally and mentally anchored to what’s in it. So if you come back after the LOI and say, “I want to tweak the purchase price, reduce the seller note, and add a consulting agreement,” the other side hears: “I’m trying to renegotiate what we already agreed on.” Now, they’re defensive. The energy shifts. And you’ve lost your flexibility. Before the LOI: All the Levers Are on the Table LOI is your golden window. It’s the only stage where: You’re exploring. You have multiple trade-offs available. Nobody’s committed yet. And both sides are more open to creativity because nothing feels “final.” That’s when you can say: “If you need that higher topline number, maybe we shift some of it to an earnout.” “If you’re worried about staff retention, let’s make that part of the consulting arrangement.” “If cash at close isn’t where you want it, what if we sweeten the seller note with a higher interest rate and shorter term?” This is where package bargaining lives—not in legal docs, but in strategic conversations between two people trying to make the puzzle fit.

It’s your last and best chance to think holistically about the deal. Because once that letter goes out with a price and a basic structure, you’ve taken a hundred other structures off the table. You’ve told the seller, “Here’s the shape of what I’m offering,” and anything that doesn’t fit inside that shape now feels like a problem. So before you send it, do your packaging. Example 1: The Seller Note Squeeze If the bank is only willing to finance the deal if there’s at least a 10% seller note involved. But the seller’s allergic to that idea—“I’m not your bank,” they say, rolling their eyes across the conference room table. Here’s a potential solution: You sweeten the seller’s consulting agreement to offset the ding. Maybe you increase their monthly rate. Maybe you give them a guaranteed six-month runway post-close with a clear scope of work. That turns the sting of the seller note into something that feels more like earned income—not deferred payment with risk attached. Want to go further? You slap a healthy interest rate on the seller note and tie it to a friendly repayment window (e.g., paid off in 18 months, not five years). That not only creates financial incentive for the seller to want the business to succeed—it also signals that you plan to prioritize paying them off quickly. Same seller note, totally different emotional experience. Example 2: The Purchase Price Bridge Radha was an attorney looking to acquire a boutique estate planning firm in Austin. The seller, Lara, had built the firm from the ground up over two decades and was proud of the client base she’d cultivated—mostly high-net-worth families and business owners with complex estate planning needs. Radha, however, was pragmatic. Based on her analysis of the financials, recurring revenue, and team capacity, she believed the practice was worth about $900,000. Lara was firm on $1.25 million, pointing to the strong pipeline of referrals, long-term client relationships, and her belief that the next 12 months were going to be her most profitable yet. Rather than argue over the valuation—or worse, walk away—they found common ground using package bargaining. Here’s how it played out: Radha agreed to pay $900,000 at closing, and they structured a $350,000 promissory note, but with a retention adjustment built in. “If the firm hits $700,000 in gross revenue in the first 12 months,” Radha said, “you’ll get the full $350,000. But if we fall short, the amount adjusts downward based on actual performance.” This allowed Lara to stand behind her confidence in the firm’s future—and Radha to protect herself from overpaying based on potential that hadn’t yet materialized. As it turned out, the firm performed well, but not quite at Lara’s forecast. Radha ended up paying $225,000 on the note—so the total purchase price landed over $1.1 million. Lara walked away feeling respected and rewarded.

Because the best deals—the durable, high-trust, low-drama ones—are made by people who understand that you don’t win deals term-by-term. You win them by building the full picture. There are a lot of different brokers out there with a lot of different backgrounds and quality and there are some folks who view diligence and thoroughness as the enemy to a deal. I know it’s easy to say from where I’m sitting on the sidelines, but the letter of intent is also about weeding out brokers that are going to make your deal miserable. If a seller or their broker sees your thoroughness as a downside, that is a red flag that will certainly show up again before the deal is done. If you are very concerned, you can also initiate conversations by a much simpler Indication of Interest (IOI) – an IOI is often little more than an email with a purchase price and can kick off discussions that will allow you to get the information you need to move on to the point where you’re able to negotiate a full LOI. Letters of Intent: Make It STRUCTURED Historically, the Letter of Intent has functioned more like a wink than a contract. It says, “We like you. Let’s see where this goes.” And for billion-dollar acquirers with deal teams and deep pockets, that might be enough. They can afford to churn through half-baked LOIs and let broken deals be a cost of doing business. And it often hides the “gotchas” that only surface halfway through diligence—when tempers are short and the champagne has gone flat. Worse, many standard LOIs are wildly one-sided. They often bind the seller through exclusivity, while letting the buyer keep every possible “out.” The result? Nail Your LOI by Making It STRUCTURED A strong LOI isn’t vague. It’s not a “we’ll figure it out later” document. It sets the tone, the timeline, and the trust level for the entire deal. That means you want to cover the key points up front. Here’s what that looks like, mapped to the STRUCTURED acronym: S – Structure Spell out exactly what’s being acquired—assets vs. equity, full sale or partial, and whether IP, brand, or real estate are included. T – Terms That Bind Clarify which terms are binding and which aren’t. Commonly binding provisions include exclusivity, confidentiality, governing law, and the agreement to negotiate in good faith. R – Retention and Price Adjustments Include any retention-based adjustments to price. Will compensation be held back if clients or employees leave? How will working capital be handled? U – Use of Employees Be explicit about employee expectations post-close—especially when the “employee” is a spouse, adult child, or a “seasonal helper.” These family-tied roles can quietly unravel deals if not addressed early. C – Covenants Not to Compete, Carveouts & the Art of Getting Specific Define the non-compete, non-solicit, and any exceptions. A vague non-compete is a lawsuit waiting to happen—or a worthless clause. Use clear terms and include carveouts where appropriate. T – Tenant Issues If there’s a lease involved, it needs real attention. What are the current rates? Are they market-based? Will the buyer assume the lease, or is a new agreement needed? Office space often becomes a surprise deal-killer when left vague. U – Use of Seller Post-Closing Outline exactly what role (if any) the seller will have post-close. Will they consult? For how long? Paid or unpaid? On call or hands-on? R – Reps, Warranties & The Legal Stuff Even if the LOI isn’t the place to draft all the reps and warranties, it should define who will prepare the purchase agreement, what laws will govern, and whether indemnification will be on the table. E – Exclusivity and Good Faith Deposits Will the seller stop shopping the deal while diligence is happening? For how long? Is there a deposit? Is it refundable? Spell it out. Chapter X: Why the LOI Is the Real Negotiation Battlefield There’s a persistent myth in the world of buying and selling businesses that a Letter of Intent (LOI) is “a placeholder”—a soft, informal gesture before the “real” negotiation starts. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard someone say, “Oh, it’s non-binding anyway.” Let me set the record straight: that’s not actually how it works. What makes a document binding or not binding isn’t the title—it’s the language inside and the way the parties act about it. In fact, if you’re doing it right, the LOI is where the real negotiation happens. This is the blueprint for the deal. Get it wrong here, and you’re in for a mess. Get it right, and everything else becomes smoother and more predictable. BOX A Quick Note on Retrades “I don’t know what to say, I guess I have to reserve the right to get smarter.” – a genius and very likeable opposing counsel telling me he wanted to change a term from the LOI Retrading — trying to change the terms after they’ve already been agreed to — is like ordering your hamburger, waiting until it hits the table, then asking the server to make it well-done instead-oh and does that bun have gluten in it? I’m gluten free. Technically, they can take it back to the kitchen, but now the chef’s annoyed, the timing’s off, and the whole experience lost its flavor. You might get what you want, but not without burning some goodwill and you’re certainly going to need to leave a bigger tip. Do it once or twice, maybe you survive. More than that and you’re going to have some serious relationship management to do. That’s why we bake as much as possible into the LOI. Reps and warranties? Those can come later. Diligence checklists? Definitely. But the terms at the heart of the deal — what everyone cares about most — should already be on the table, talked through, and agreed upon before you sign exclusivity. Next, we’ll break down what each structure really means, and why it matters. [add a drawing where someone either buys a black box or gets to open that box and choose what they want to buy out of it] Asset Purchase: The Pick-and-Choose Approach In an asset purchase, the buyer forms a new entity—let’s call it “Newco”—and purchases selected assets from the selling business. These might include physical property (like equipment and furniture), intangible property (like trademarks, customer lists, and goodwill), or contracts, inventory, and licenses. The seller retains the corporate shell—and, under the general rule, also retains the liabilities. That’s a big reason why asset purchases are the go-to choice for many buyers: they get what they want, without taking on what they don’t. But before you get too comfortable, know this: the general rule about avoiding liabilities has several exceptions, and they’re not rare. Successor Liability: What Buyers Hope to Avoid... But Sometimes Can’t In most asset deals, the legal default is that the buyer does not inherit the seller’s debts, lawsuits, or liabilities. Those remain with the selling entity. But courts can and do pop this bubble of protection (called piercing the corporate veil) under certain circumstances. Here are the major exceptions to keep in mind: 1. De Facto Merger If the transaction walks and talks like a merger—even if it’s called an asset purchase—a court may treat it as one. This can happen when: The seller’s business continues substantially unchanged under the buyer The same officers or owners stay involved in similar roles and/or There’s little separation between the old and new entities 2. Express or Implied Assumption of Liability If the buyer contractually agrees to take on certain debts—or behaves in a way that implies it has assumed them—those liabilities may follow them. This could happen with informal actions like continuing to pay off old vendor contracts or covering warranties without a formal agreement. 3. Fraudulent Transfer If a deal is structured in a way that appears to be an attempt to avoid creditors—by stripping the seller of its valuable assets and leaving it unable to meet obligations—courts can undo the transaction. This is especially risky when: No real consideration (money or value) was exchanged There is overlap in ownership or management The buyer continues operations using the same staff, location, or branding 4. Product Line Exception Some states apply the product line exception, particularly in manufacturing cases. If the buyer continues producing the same product line, they may be held liable for claims arising from products sold before the purchase—even if it was technically an asset deal. 5. Labor and Employment Law Even where general successor liability doesn’t apply, certain labor laws may impose obligations on a buyer—especially when the buyer hires a majority of the seller’s workforce and continues operating in the same fashion. Stock Purchase: Simpler for the Seller, Riskier for the Buyer In a stock purchase, the buyer acquires the ownership interests—shares, units, or membership interests—in the selling company itself. The business entity doesn’t change. Contracts, licenses, employees, and (crucially) liabilities all remain intact. That continuity can make for a smoother transition—there’s no name change, no need to re-assign leases, licenses, or vendor agreements, you can keep the same bank account—but it also means the buyer inherits everything, including unknown or contingent liabilities. This structure often appeals to sellers, since it minimizes disruption and can offer more favorable tax treatment. But buyers need to tread carefully, often with thorough due diligence and indemnity protections built into the purchase agreement. Some of it might be old, uncollectible, or tied up in disputes.

BOX Accounts Receivable Asset Purchase vs. Stock Purchase: What Happens to Accounts Receivable? One of the key differences between an asset purchase and a stock purchase comes down to what you’re buying—and accounts receivable is a perfect example of how that plays out in the real world. In an Asset Purchase The buyer is only acquiring specific assets and liabilities that are listed in the purchase agreement. Think of it like a “pick-and-choose” deal. If you’re the buyer, you might choose to buy the client list, equipment, goodwill, and lease—but usually not the accounts receivable. Why? Because A/R can be a bit messy. Some of it might be old, uncollectible, or tied up in disputes. In many cases, the seller keeps their own receivables, continues to collect them after closing, and may even pay the buyer a percentage if any work is required to help with collections. In a Stock Purchase You’re buying the whole company entity, liabilities and all. That includes the corporate shell, contracts, obligations—and yes, accounts receivable. In this case, the A/R is part of the business’s balance sheet at closing. It becomes yours, for better or worse. If there’s $100K in outstanding invoices, they’re now yours to collect. But so are any aging receivables, billing disputes, or accounting quirks that haven’t been cleaned up. Bottom line: In a stock deal, you inherit the A/R by default—so you better be confident in what you’re getting. BOX Tax Treatment: The IRS Cares How You Structure Your Deal Deal structure doesn’t just influence liability exposure—it directly affects how the transaction is taxed for both parties. Asset Purchase – Tax Implications Both parties must file IRS Form 8594, which allocates the purchase price across categories like tangible property, inventory, goodwill, and non-compete agreements. These allocations affect the buyer’s future deductions and the seller’s tax liabilities. As a general rule, Sellers are going to want as much allocated to goodwill as possible to maximize the amount of the purchase price they’ll be paying capital gains on (versus a worse ordinary income tax) Buyer’s advantage: Buyers get a stepup in basis. That means they can depreciate or amortize assets based on their fair market value, which can create significant tax deductions over time. Seller’s challenge: For C corporations, asset sales often result in double taxation—first at the corporate level when assets are sold, and again when proceeds are distributed to shareholders. Even in pass-through entities, certain assets (like depreciated equipment) can trigger ordinary income, which is taxed at higher rates than capital gains. Stock Purchase – Tax Implications Seller’s benefit: Typically, the seller pays capital gains tax on the sale of the ownership interest—often at favorable long-term rates. Buyer’s limitation: The buyer takes over the company “as-is,” including its historical basis in assets. That means less depreciation or amortization benefit compared to an asset purchase. Choosing the Right Structure Here’s the general pattern: Buyers tend to prefer asset purchases for the ability to avoid liabilities and step up basis. Sellers often push for stock sales to simplify the transition and optimize tax outcomes. But every deal is unique. The right choice depends on: The type of business The parties' tax positions The existence of contracts or licenses that are hard to assign The tolerance for risk Whether you're buying or selling, deal structure matters. A lot. It shapes risk exposure, tax liability, and how cleanly the business transitions to its next chapter. And while asset purchases are often seen as the “safer” option, they don’t provide a free pass. Courts look at substance over form. If the facts suggest the deal was a merger in disguise or designed to evade liabilities, successor liability can follow. T- Terms that Bind- What’s Binding and What’s Not? [figure of shackles on different terms] A typical LOI is a mix of binding and non-binding provisions. And the trick is being crystal clear about which is which. Courts look to the intent of the parties—what you agreed to, not what you called it. Here’s how it usually breaks down: Binding Provisions These are the parts that are enforceable immediately, regardless of whether the final purchase agreement ever gets signed. Common binding clauses include: Confidentiality This protects sensitive business information exchanged during due diligence. It means you can’t take what you learn about the other party and use it to compete, leak it, or shop it around. Exclusivity (also called a “no-shop” clause) This gives the buyer a set period of time where the seller agrees not to entertain other offers or shop the deal elsewhere. It’s binding, and violating it can tank trust—and trigger legal consequences. Governing Law This tells everyone which state’s laws will apply if there’s a dispute.

In practice, once something is in the LOI, it becomes emotionally and practically difficult to change. Any shift can look like a re-trade, and that erodes trust. there are court cases where Letters of Intent (LOIs) were treated as binding contracts, despite their typical non-binding language. Courts often look beyond the document’s label and evaluate the intent of the parties, the language used, and their conduct. Here’s a quick breakdown: When an LOI Can Be Treated as Binding Courts may enforce an LOI—or portions of it—if: The language indicates intent to be bound, even provisionally. Key deal terms (like price, closing date, or payment structure) are sufficiently defined. The parties acted as if they had a deal, e.g., starting performance, sharing confidential data, or excluding other offers. There’s evidence of reliance or partial performance that creates equitable grounds for enforcement (like promissory estoppel). Key Cases Where LOIs Were Treated as Binding Teachers Insurance & Annuity Association v. Tribune Co., 670 F. Supp. 491 (S.D.N.Y. 1987) The court found that the parties intended to be bound by the LOI, even though some terms were still being negotiated. Critical takeaway: A detailed LOI with agreed-upon material terms may signal an intent to be bound. Texaco, Inc. v. Pennzoil Co., 729 S.W.2d 768 (Tex. App. 1987) One of the most famous: Pennzoil and Getty had a signed Memorandum of Agreement, but Texaco swooped in before a formal contract was signed. Jury found a binding agreement existed, leading to a $10+ billion verdict against Texaco. Empro Mfg. Co. v. Ball-Co Manufacturing, Inc., 870 F.2d 423 (7th Cir. 1989) The opposite result: court ruled the LOI was non-binding, largely because it expressly disclaimed any obligation to close until a formal agreement was signed. Avoid acting like the deal is done before it is (e.g., don’t announce it or start integration). Example: Non-binding Nature. Except for the provisions relating to exclusivity, confidentiality, governing law, and any other specifically designated binding terms, this Letter of Intent is non-binding and does not create any legally enforceable obligations on either party to consummate the transaction. R-Retention Adjustments – Aligning Incentives & Creating a Bridge When used well, retention adjustments can offer a clean way to lower the risk of a deal without getting too far into legal weeds and without adverse tax consequences. Let’s unpack what this is, when to use it, and what you need to watch out for. What Is a Retention Adjustment? A retention adjustment is a mechanism that adjusts the purchase price down after closing if certain client or revenue thresholds aren’t met during the transition period. It’s usually tied to the retention of key clients, staff, or recurring revenue, and instead of being paid extra for hitting targets (like in an earnout), the seller takes a reduction if those targets aren’t met. In short: It’s not a bonus for performance—it’s a discount for underperformance. These adjustments are typically structured as: Reductions to the seller note principal Purchase price offsets or clawbacks held in escrow Discounts built into a final installment payment due after a short transition It’s an elegant way to align incentives during the handoff—especially when the seller insists that “the clients will stay” or “the staff loves me and they’ll be fine.” If they’re that confident, they shouldn’t balk. [Box: The SBA 7(a) Problem: No Post-Closing Seller Upside If you’re financing the deal with an SBA 7(a) loan, your options get more limited—fast. The SBA has strict rules about no post-closing seller upside. That traditionally meant: No earnouts No performance-based bonuses No “phantom equity” or backend kicker Their rationale is that they don’t want the seller continuing to influence the business in a way that might jeopardize the buyer’s ability to operate independently. It’s also about loan collateralization and repayment certainty. But downside-only adjustments? Technically allowed. You can include mechanisms that reduce the purchase price if certain conditions aren't met, as long as they’re clearly defined at the time of closing and don’t function like earnouts in disguise. That said, just because you can do it doesn’t mean everyone will like it. Why Downside-Only Adjustments Can Rub Sellers the Wrong Way Here’s where deal psychology kicks in. Even though a retention adjustment is technically fair—“If the clients don’t stay, I’m not paying full price”—it often feels worse to sellers than a traditional earnout. Why? Because it’s all risk, no reward. Earnouts say: “Hey, you could make even more!” Retention adjustments say: “We’re docking your pay if things go sideways.” And if you’re layering this onto a deal that already has a heavy seller note, consulting agreement, or SBA scrutiny? It can start to feel punitive—especially to a seller who already has to wait 3–5 years to get fully paid.] So, when you use retention adjustments, clarity and tone matter. Here’s how to do it well: How to Structure a Retention Adjustment That Doesn’t Torpedo the Deal Tie it to a clear metric. Think: “Client X, Y, and Z stay through Month 12” or “$400K of revenue from recurring clients remains billed by Month 18.” Fuzzy metrics = instant red flags. Numerator: Start with the numerator—that’s what the seller gets credit for retaining. Is it gross revenue? Specific client names? A revenue figure tied only to recurring services? You want clarity here. If it’s based on revenue, is it collected revenue or billed revenue? The more precise this is, the less room there is for misunderstanding (or manipulation) down the road. I usually prefer topline targets like gross revenue because the buyer can control the costs/overhead. As an example of how manipulatable EBTIDA or profit is, if you have a metric tied to profit margin, the buyer may be able to add a consulting fee to an affiliate entity in there to wipe out any profit. Because of this, you have to get granular on your definition of what counts as qualified overhead to keep that type of manipulation at bay. While doable, that’s a hefty negotiation point to add into a smaller deal and the attorneys’ fees can stack up. Additionally, a narrow definition of what counts as profit can have unintended consequences that keep the buyer from running the business the way they should in their best judgment. Better to stick to topline. Next, the denominator—the baseline. This is what the retention is measured against. It could be total trailing twelve months (TTM) revenue, a list of clients included in the deal, or the average of the last three years. Sellers need to ensure that the denominator reflects the actual strength of the business they’re selling—not a cherry-picked high point that sets them up to fail.

U- Use of Seller Post-Closing (Or: That Alaskan Cruise May Need to Wait) One of the most overlooked, most awkward, and most important dynamics in any small business acquisition is this question: What exactly is the seller doing after this deal closes? Because here’s the thing: the seller may be picturing a six-month cruise, Mai Tai in hand, no emails, no client calls, and absolutely no staff questions. But you? You might be expecting them to sit in on every single client handoff, meet weekly for strategy sessions, and maybe even stick around long enough to help train their replacement. If those visions don’t match? Congratulations, you’re about to hit your first major post-close expectation clash. Why You Have to Talk About This Before You Sign When someone sells their business, part of what the buyer is paying for is them—or at least, the value they’ve built around their name, their relationships, and their know-how. That goodwill is baked into the purchase price. So yes, some amount of post-closing help is expected and totally fair. Things like introducing the buyer to key clients, being available to answer questions, and helping them understand how the firm runs day to day—that’s all part of the deal. No one expects a seller to hand over the keys and disappear into the sunset the next morning (well, unless that was the agreement). But here’s the important part: there’s a line. Once a seller has given a reasonable amount of time and effort to support the transition, anything beyond that should be treated as additional work—and compensated accordingly. If a seller is answering emails at midnight three months after closing, or being asked to handle shift work like they never left, it’s no longer a “transition.” It’s free labor. And that’s when things get weird. So when structuring a deal, it’s important to talk about this early. The parties should agree on what’s included in the purchase price in terms of the seller’s time and involvement, and then draw a clear boundary.

Why Would the Landlord Say Yes? Think about it from the landlord’s perspective. Right now, they have a tenant with: A long-standing history of paying rent An existing business or personal relationship A lease they probably like (or at least tolerate) Now you’re asking them to: Let that tenant off the hook (often years before the lease ends) Replace them with a new person who has no track record in that location Agree to new lease terms, often with bank-mandated clauses they hate Pay legal fees to draft or review a lease assignment they didn’t ask for [Box SBA Oh, and if the deal is SBA-financed? Why? Because that $1 gets paid monthly—and over the life of a 5- or 10-year lease, that’s serious cash flow. The seller walks away with a tidy income stream, often taxed favorably. That’s why smart sellers will always push a buyer to “raise the rent a little” rather than shave the purchase price. This is exactly why we don’t take terms off the table too early. Because the lease and the purchase price are linked—you move one, the other moves too. Package bargaining at its finest. A broker colleague once told me: “I won’t sell a business if a key employee wanted to buy it but couldn’t. Those deals almost always implode.” Why? Because resentment poisons transitions. Thanks to SBA 7(a) loans and thanks to private equity’s impact on the market, buyers can often purchase a business with only 10% down. That sounds great—unless you’re a retiring parent who’s counting on the proceeds to fund retirement. Selling to your kid means: Taking less money and funding their loan yourself, AND Asking them to shoulder millions in debt they probably can't afford. In either scenario, tensions rise. The seller can’t afford to turn down millions right at the cusp of their retirement and the family member employee can’t afford to take on millions in debt. The family member employee may stay on, but often they’re bitter. They feel overlooked. And when the buyer shows up, they’re walking into a landmine. Ask how that person feels about the transition. And have a plan—whether that’s a buyout path, a defined role, or a timeline for their exit. Sometimes she’s the de facto HR department—onboarding employees, handling payroll questions, even smoothing over office drama. Other times, she’s doing serious work that no one thought to mention. One time, it was a plumbing company where the spouse was doing all the bookkeeping—and doing it well. Another time, it was a gym where the seller’s wife was training clients several days a week... without taking a dime in salary. Here’s the issue: that labor isn’t reflected in the financials. What looked like a solid 25% margin on paper might really be 15% once the free labor is accounted for. This isn’t about pointing fingers—it’s about uncovering the real picture. Not the promises, but the actual paperwork that transfers money, responsibility, risk, and assets. They get to: Choose the structure and tone of the agreement Decide what’s “included” vs. what has to be negotiated Build in subtle risk allocations—often buried in reps, warranties, and indemnities Even if the other side redlines it to death, the initial draft creates momentum. In the flurry of deal terms and negotiations, there’s one small section that often gets shrugged off until the very end: the governing law and jurisdiction clause. It sounds boring. It’s legal boilerplate. Who cares, right? You should care. This seemingly tiny clause can end up deciding how expensive, complicated, and winnable your dispute becomes if the deal ever blows up. Let’s break down what these two terms really mean—and why you want to think about them sooner rather than later. Governing Law: What Rules Apply? Governing law means: if there’s a dispute over the deal, which state’s laws will be used to interpret and enforce the agreement? This matters a lot more than you might think. Different states have different rules when it comes to things like: Non-competes (California hates them; Florida doesn’t mind them) Successor liability Indemnity enforceability Usury laws (affecting interest rates on seller notes) Statutes of limitations Interpretation of vague terms (some states let in a lot of parol evidence; others don’t) Confessions of Judgment Pre-dispute Jury Trial Waivers Whether employee PTO has to be paid out at closing (for an asset purchase) [Box Tip: Real Example: PTO and Governing Law Let’s say someone is drafting an LOI to buy a firm in Arizona, and they’re used to deals in states where accrued PTO doesn’t have to be paid out unless the seller’s policy says so. So they don’t address it in the LOI—they assume it’ll stay on the books post-closing, like any other accrued liability. But here’s the twist: what if it turns out the governing law is California? In California, unused PTO must be paid out at the time of termination—which includes a change in ownership where the seller’s entity is closing or employees are technically being let go. Suddenly, the seller is on the hook to write checks for every unused hour of PTO at closing, and the buyer may have to rehire those employees from scratch. If the LOI doesn’t reflect that? Now there’s a gap. Someone’s eating that cost, and it becomes a fight over whether the purchase price should be adjusted, who’s paying what, and how liabilities are being allocated. The takeaway? Always confirm the governing law early, and build key employment-related assumptions—like PTO payout—into the LOI. It might seem like a small item, but when you’re talking about dozens of employees, it adds up fast.] Jurisdiction: Where Do We Go to Argue About It? Jurisdiction answers a different but equally important question: where will the lawsuit happen if something goes wrong? This determines where someone has to physically show up and litigate the dispute—who’s traveling, which courthouse is in charge, and what rules of procedure apply. A buyer based in New York and a seller based in Georgia might choose: Georgia as jurisdiction (because the assets are there) New York (because the buyer’s likely to be the party needing to sue) Delaware (as a neutral ground, but one that both parties find equally inconvenient, and maybe that’s the point) It may sound trivial—until you realize that hiring legal counsel in another state, traveling for hearings, or being forced into a court that strongly favors local parties can shift leverage dramatically in a dispute. If you had an indemnification clause, you could say, “Hey, you told me these brakes were good. You owe me the cost to fix them.” Now imagine the “car” is a $7 million business. And What’s “Survival” Got to Do With It? Survival refers to how long the seller’s representations and warranties last after the deal closes. If a rep "survives" for 18 months, that means the buyer has 18 months to discover a breach and make a claim. Some representations should die a quick death (to give the seller certainty), but others—like those related to ownership of the business or taxes—are fundamental. Those should never expire. You should be able to bring a claim for those five years later if needed, because discovering you paid millions for a business that the seller didn’t have a right to sell you doesn’t get better with time. Here’s a good rule of thumb: 12-24 months is a reasonable survival period for most reps. No limit (infinite survival is fair) on fundamental reps like: Ownership of the business Authority to enter the agreement Tax liabilities Environmental or legal compliance (sometimes) Why Survival and Indemnification Belong in the LOI (At Least a Little Bit) Look, I get it. You don’t want to negotiate every detail in the LOI. It’s non-binding, the lawyers haven’t even been hired yet, and the buyer and seller are playing nice. But that’s exactly why this is the time to plant the flag—before people get defensive. If the seller is going to demand a $10 liability cap or wants all reps to expire on the day of closing, you need to know that before you waste a dime on due diligence. Common Reps and Warranties — And Why They Matter These are the “guarantees” the seller is making about the state of the business at signing and closing. Here are the hits: Ownership of assets or stock Financial statements are accurate No undisclosed liabilities Compliance with laws No lawsuits or threatened claims Contracts are valid and assignable Taxes have been filed and paid All necessary consents have been obtained If any of those turn out to be false, the buyer can make a claim—but only if the survival period hasn’t lapsed and the breach wasn’t carved out of indemnification. [Box Tip In an asset purchase, the seller is often a company that will close up shop after the deal closes. It’ll be gutted. The assets are gone. It has no revenue. Maybe not even a bank account. So if something goes wrong and you try to collect on that indemnity promise—good luck suing a shell. The legal term for this is “piercing the corporate veil,” and courts don’t hand that out like candy. Unless you can prove fraud or that the company was never properly capitalized, you might be out of luck. Which is why you often want the owner themselves to sign personally—or at least to backstop the indemnity with a personal guarantee or an escrow holdback. This can be uncomfortable. But it’s also common sense. You want to know that someone has skin in the game if things go sideways. On the flip side, in a stock purchase, this issue is even more complex. After the closing, the buyer owns the seller. So when you sue for breach of reps, you’re basically suing yourself—unless you preserved a direct claim against the former owner. So again: you want that former owner on the hook. And you want that commitment spelled out clearly in the agreement (and sometimes backed by an escrow or insurance). The seller, of course, may want the buyer’s owner to personally guarant some part of the deal—like a promissory note. This isn’t always unreasonable. Exclusivity in a deal usually runs one way: the seller agrees not to shop the business around while the buyer does their diligence and works toward closing. It’s not standard—or expected—for the buyer to be exclusive. Buyers are often evaluating multiple opportunities at once, and that’s generally accepted. The exclusivity is there to protect the buyer’s time and money, not to tie their hands. “You, seller, agree not to see other buyers while I, buyer, do the work and spend the money to figure out if this relationship should turn into a full-blown acquisition.” That’s the clean version. But what exclusivity really does is buy the buyer time—and signal to the seller that the buyer is serious. What Is an Exclusivity Provision? It’s a period of time (usually 30–90 days) during which: The seller agrees not to negotiate with or solicit offers from other potential buyers The buyer gets access to diligence materials and begins working toward closing The buyer attempts to secure financing Both sides attempt to finalize the terms outlined in the LOI in the definitive agreements In theory, it’s a mutual trust exercise. In practice, it’s the moment where both sides feel slightly nervous. Buyers are thinking: “I don’t want to waste money on legal fees and diligence only to lose the deal to a last-minute higher bidder.” Sellers are thinking: “I don’t want to get strung along for three months by a buyer who’s not really serious and just wants to look under the hood.” So how do you make it fair? The Great Debate: Good Faith Deposits Here’s where things get spicy. Should a buyer put down a good faith deposit during exclusivity? If I’m the seller: Absolutely. Even a small deposit ($10,000–$15,000) shows seriousness. It forces the buyer to pause before ghosting (meaning disappearing with no notice but not telling someone they’re no longer into the deal). It compensates for the risk of taking the business off the market. If I’m the buyer: No thanks. I’m not committing cash until I know the financials check out. I’ll already usually be committing time and resources, but even more money? That feels premature. Where I’ve landed, after watching enough deals implode? If there’s going to be exclusivity and I’m repping the seller, I usually want some kind of deposit—not because it guarantees anything, but because it keeps both parties honest and encourages the buyer to give notice promptly if they’re cooling on the deal. Buyers who have cash on the line are far less likely to disappear. And that alone can be worth the exercise. If someone’s going to bail, better to find out as soon as you can. Exclusivity can be a blank canvas, but here are some common—and smart—add-ons: Milestone-based exclusivity: The exclusivity period auto-extends as long as the buyer is meeting key milestones (loan application submitted, diligence completed, APA drafted, etc.) Reimbursement rights: If one party backs out in bad faith, the other can recoup a set amount of costs (legal, accounting, etc.) Liquidated damages: Rare, but in higher-stakes deals, there may be a predefined fee owed if the deal is tanked without valid cause (as you can imagine, this is a heavily debated term and, frankly, in small deals will not be worth the legal spend to negotiate it) Deposit refund triggers: The buyer gets their deposit back only if certain conditions aren’t met (e.g., undisclosed liabilities, material misstatements, inability to secure financing) I’m okay with these as long as the goal is alignment—not punishment. We’re not in the forced deal business. In small business, business is personal. If someone doesn’t want to sell—or doesn’t want to buy—you don’t want to hold them hostage. That usually doesn’t end well. A good exclusivity provision does three things: Gives the buyer a real window to explore the deal without worrying about other offers popping up Gives the seller confidence they’re not being played for time Aligns both parties around timelines, behavior, and seriousness That’s it. And if one side needs out? Let them out. There are deals that fall apart because they should—and trying to strong-arm someone into closing is the best way to make a bad deal worse.
