But there’s a reason for that. In our STRUCTURED framework, price comes after we’ve nailed down the structure, terms, roles, and risks—because the number only makes sense in context and it’s important not to skip to the topline number too fast. Think of it like building a house. You wouldn’t agree on the total cost before knowing how many bedrooms, what kind of foundation, or whether you’re including a pool. Same goes here. The purchase price is the outcome of everything else in the deal—the business model, the cash flow, the deal structure, the risks each side is taking on, and the terms they’re willing to live with. So yes, price matters. And yes it matters a lot. But the purchase price only makes sense in the context of the deal. (How to Establish a Purchase Price Without Sleeping with the Fishes) When it comes to buying an accounting firm (my specialty)—or really any small business—the most common question I get from buyers is: “How do I figure out what to offer?” And my answer is always the same: you’ve got to call in the MAFIA. No, not that mafia. No one’s getting whacked here. I’m talking about the silly but memorable framework I use with clients to price deals like a professional—M.A.F.I.A. It’s memorable, it’s effective, and yes, it comes with terrible Godfather joke opportunities. So, let’s break down the MAFIA acronym: M — Market: What’s the Demand? Start with the basics: who else wants this business? You’re not negotiating in a vacuum. If this firm has a dozen interested buyers and an active broker marketing it nationally, you’re playing in a seller’s market. If it’s been sitting stale on a listing site for eighteen months with no bites and the seller changed the font on their CIM, hoping no one would notice. That’s a buyer’s market. Ask questions like: How many other buyers have signed NDAs? Has anyone already made an offer and walked? How long has it been listed? The heat in the market will tell you a lot about how aggressive—or conservative—your offer needs to be. A — Adjusted EBITDA (or SDE for smaller firms) This is the engine of your offer. Forget “gross revenue”—you want to know what the business earns after you adjust for owner perks, one-time expenses, and anomalies. SDE vs. EBITDA: Know Who You Are in the Deal Here’s a simple rule of thumb: if you’re buying the business to run it yourself, you care about SDE. If you’re not, and someone else is going to run it, then EBITDA is your metric. Most deals under $5 million in value are what we call owner-operator deals—you’re stepping into the seller’s shoes, managing the team, maybe even doing some of the client work. In that case, you look at Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE) because it reflects what the business puts in your pocket. SDE adds back things like the seller’s salary, personal expenses, and one-time costs—so it gives a more accurate picture of the cash flow you, as the new owner/operator, can expect to live on. But if you’re planning to be a hands-off owner—or you’re institutional or private equity-backed—you’re going to need to hire someone to run the business. That means you care about EBITDA, which is earnings before compensation for the operator. You’ll be paying someone a salary to do what the seller used to do, so SDE isn’t a real number for you—it’s inflated. EBITDA gives you a cleaner, more scalable view of performance if you're not planning to be in the trenches yourself. Bottom line: Know who you’re going to be in the deal. The operator? SDE. The investor? EBITDA. Don’t confuse the two—it leads to overpaying and serious headaches. One of the biggest early misunderstandings in a deal comes down to a deceptively simple number: the asking price. It’s important to understand that the asking price is not always the same as the seller’s “want” price. The asking price is what’s listed. It’s the number they’re putting out there publicly—sometimes to anchor the conversation high, sometimes to signal a certain level of seriousness. But the want price? That’s what the seller needs or hopes to walk away with when it’s all said and done. As a buyer, it’s worth respecting the asking price if you can—it sets the tone for the negotiation and shows you’re approaching the deal in good faith. That doesn’t mean you can’t negotiate. But anchoring way below the ask right out of the gate can derail conversations before they even begin, especially in deals where relationships matter. That said, part of your job in diligence and deal structuring is to gently work your way toward that want price—the number the seller has told themselves they have to have after taxes, fees, and financing. You’re not just trying to get a good deal; you’re trying to create one that works for both sides. Smart buyers aim for alignment—not friction.

Great. But don’t celebrate yet. Because the next question the seller’s going to ask—either out loud or silently while staring at your LOI—is this: “How much of that am I getting at close?” This is where buyers often fumble. They think the purchase price is the headline. But in reality, the structure of how that price is paid matters as much—if not more—to the seller. Rare is a seller who would prefer 3M in an earnout over 2.8M cash at closing. Put differently: 3 million dollars isn’t always worth 3 million dollars. To a seller, $2.8M cash at close might feel way better—and be way more appealing—than a $3M offer where half is in an earnout tied to three years of client retention and one mild gust of wind. Why? Because certainty matters. Finality matters. Getting paid now, not later (and not maybe later) matters. Especially for sellers who are walking into retirement, paying off debt, or emotionally trying to let go of something they’ve built for decades. So when you’re presenting your purchase price, you need to break it down clearly: Cash at closing (What hits their account day one?) Seller Note (How much is deferred, and what are the terms?) Earnout/Contingencies (What’s performance-based, and how do they earn it?) Equity rollover/Equity Grant (Are they retaining any stake in the business or getting paid in any equity of another business?) And then ask yourself: “Would I take this deal if I were them?” If your offer is heavy on future-based compensation—like earnouts, consulting fees, or equity that might pay off “someday”—you’d better have a good reason and a compelling story to sell it. Otherwise, you’re pitching risk in a tuxedo. This doesn’t mean you have to offer 100% cash. But it does mean you need to understand the emotional weight of the payout structure. Because a technically higher offer that’s back-loaded with conditions doesn’t always win. Want to close the deal? Deliver the price in a way that respects the seller’s need for clarity, dignity, and a clean break—when that’s what they’re looking for. And if they aren’t looking for a clean break? Even better. Seller Note How much is deferred, and what are the terms? A seller note is basically: “You finance part of your own exit, and I’ll pay you back over time with interest.” It’s a way to stretch the purchase price without overloading on bank debt. It often includes: An interest rate (usually 5–8%) A payment term (1–5 years) Regular monthly or quarterly payments Sometimes comes with a portion on standby to allow the Buyer to get the business stabilized post-Closing before payments begin. The benefit? It aligns incentives. The seller has skin in the game post-close and a reason to support a smooth transition. The downside (from the seller’s view)? It’s riskier than cash. If the buyer fails, the note may not get paid. Use when: The bank or investment group wants you to have more seller skin in the game You want to reduce your upfront cash burden You want to keep the seller motivated to help you with a smooth transition Pro tip: Sweeten the deal with an interest rate that makes it feel like a smart investment—not a forced concession. [Box Note on Interest Rates: Why 0% Seller Notes Aren’t Really a Thing It might sound simple and clean: “Let’s do a 0% seller note. No interest, no problem, right?” Not so fast. In the eyes of the IRS, a 0% note isn’t really a 0% note. Thanks to the imputed interest rules under Section 1274 of the Internal Revenue Code, the government assumes that any seller financing includes a minimum level of interest—even if the contract says otherwise. That minimum is tied to something called the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR), which is published monthly by the IRS. So what happens if you sign a seller note with 0% interest? The IRS steps in and says, “Cool story, but we’re going to pretend this note does have interest—and we’re going to tax the seller as if they received it.” In other words, the seller could owe taxes on income they never received. And the buyer doesn’t get an interest deduction either, because no interest was technically paid. It’s a lose-lose scenario, and that’s why zero-interest notes are not regularly used in real deals. If the goal is to keep the overall price or payments low, it’s better to work within the rules—use a low but reasonable interest rate (typically at or above the AFR), and structure the deal in a way that keeps both parties protected and tax-compliant.] 3bi Lender Protections Commonly Used in Seller Notes Seller financing can be a powerful way to bridge valuation gaps, smooth out closing logistics, or share risk—but if you’re the seller, it’s worth looking closely at the structure of the note, not the number on the page. Seller notes are not all created equal. Let’s look at the range: A contingent, subordinated, non-guaranteed, non-collateralized 10-year note? That’s a promissory note in name only. It’s long, unsecured, dependent on future events, and there's no personal guarantee if things go sideways. That’s the “you’ll get paid if everything goes well” and it’s stressful. On the flip side, a personally guaranteed, collateralized 2-year note with no contingency and no subordination? That’s real paper. It’s short-term, secured by assets, and backed by someone’s personal promise to pay. If things go wrong, you have legal recourse and leverage. It’s not cash, but it’s maybe the next best thing. Lenders use layers of protection to reduce risk, and you should too. Some of the most common protections built into seller notes include: Personal Guarantees – The buyer is personally on the hook if the entity can’t pay. Collateral – The note is secured by assets (often the business itself), giving the seller recourse if there’s a default. Shorter Terms – Less time means less risk. A two-year note is far more secure than a 10-year slow drip. No Contingencies – Fixed payments are better than ones tied to revenue, retention, or other post-closing performance metrics.

Security Interest in Business Assets What it does: Gives the seller a legal claim over the business’s assets (e.g., receivables, equipment, goodwill) in the event of default. How it's done: Via a Security Agreement + UCC-1 filing. Why it matters: Puts the seller ahead of unsecured creditors in bankruptcy or collection. 2. Acceleration Clause What it does: Allows the seller to demand the entire unpaid balance if the buyer defaults. Why it matters: Prevents drawn-out delinquency and gives the seller a clear enforcement path. 3. Default Interest Rate What it does: Triggers a higher interest rate (e.g., an additional 2–5%) if payments are missed or late. Why it matters: Incentivizes on-time payments and compensates for added risk after default. 4. Late Payment Penalties / Fees What it does: Adds a fixed fee or percentage (e.g., $250 or 5%) if a payment is late by more than X days. Why it matters: Reinforces the importance of timely payments and offsets admin costs. 5. Personal Guarantee (if buyer is an entity) What it does: Makes at least one individual behind the entity personally responsible for the debt. Why it matters: Reduces the risk of hiding behind a shell company or dissolving the buyer entity to dodge repayment. 6. Confession of Judgment (jurisdiction-dependent) What it does: Allows the seller to obtain a court judgment without a trial if the buyer defaults. Why it matters: Fast enforcement—but controversial and often restricted by law. See Appendix X for more detail than you ever thought you’d want on a Confession of Judgment. 7. Balloon Payment or Front-Loaded Payments What it does: Requires more money up front or a lump sum at the end to limit risk exposure and to encourage the noteholder to refinance debt to pay off the loan in a timely fashion. Why it matters: Reduces the outstanding balance quickly or provides a final incentive for full performance. 8. Why it matters: Gives the seller more oversight and remedies if the buyer mismanages the business. 9. Earnouts and purchase price retention adjustments can look similar on the surface—both involve the seller getting paid after closing—but they serve very different purposes. A retention adjustment is typically tied to the value the buyer thought they were buying—usually based on how much revenue or how many clients stick around after closing. It’s a way to protect the buyer if the business doesn’t perform as expected right out of the gate. [BOX Working Capital Isn’t a Mystery—It’s a Math Problem (Don’t Get Cute With It) Let’s have a quick grown-up conversation about working capital. This is one of those terms that gets thrown around in due diligence like everyone knows what it means—but when you ask people to define it or model it? You get a lot of squinting and throat clearing. So let’s make it simple: working capital is the money your business needs to function the day after closing. It covers the bills that come due before the next check hits the bank. Payroll. Rent. Software subscriptions. You know, the oxygen to keep the fire burning. Here’s the trick: working capital can be quite seasonal. If the business is cyclical—like a tax-heavy CPA firm or a holiday-dependent retail business—you need to tie the working capital estimate to the closing date, not to some theoretical “average.” Closing on March 15? You’ll need more float than if you close in August. Closing right before a big accounts receivable payday? You may need less. In other words, don’t guess. Model it. Ask the seller’s bookkeeper to pull 12-month trailing working capital snapshots. Then adjust to fit your anticipated close. And please, I say this with love: don’t try to get clever or overly “creative” with working capital math. This isn’t the place to win negotiating points or flex your Excel skills. I’ve seen buyers burn goodwill over $30K of inventory—and then lose 10x that in trust and deal fatigue. If you need working capital to close, borrow it, bake it into your financing package, and move on with your life. Deals get stuck when people haggle over things that aren’t the real issue. Don’t let working capital become a hill to die on. It’s not sexy, it’s not strategic, and if you underfund it? You’ll regret it faster than you can say “unexpected payroll gap.” ] Working Capital Checklist Check out the checklist in Appendix X for more on working capital. This is your sanity list before closing. Use it in the beginning AND AGAIN in the 30–45 days leading up to closing to make sure your numbers are right and your assumptions match the timing of the deal. It’s the blueprint for everything that comes next. And when you organize your thinking around the STRUCTURED elements, you’re not just filling in blanks—you’re asking the right questions, spotting the right pressure points, and heading off misunderstandings before they become expensive problems. Will every deal hit every letter perfectly? Probably not. That’s okay. The goal isn’t to rigidly follow the acronym—it’s to use it as a checklist, a conversation guide, and a gut check. It’s your way to make sure you're not just reacting—you’re leading. Because here’s the thing: people remember how a deal felt. And a well-structured LOI doesn’t make the deal better and more likely to close—it makes everyone at the table feel like they’re dealing with a professional who respects the process and is here to build something solid. That’s what STRUCTURED helps you do. Conclusion If you’ve made it this far, congratulations. You now know more about small business deals—especially the letter of intent—than 99% of people out there throwing offers around on firm they find on BizBuySell. But more importantly, you know that good deals aren’t found—they’re built. They’re shaped by clarity, structure, alignment, and human connection. They’re the product of real negotiation, thoughtful drafting, and an understanding that behind every spreadsheet is a person with a story. This book wasn’t meant to give you every answer. It was designed to arm you with better questions—the kind that lead to smarter terms, smoother closings, and fewer surprises six months later. Because here’s the truth: no deal is perfect. Every acquisition is a living, breathing negotiation between people who are (usually) doing this for the first and only time. But a deal doesn’t need to be perfect. It needs to be intentional. By focusing on structure, staying curious, managing deal fatigue, and using package bargaining and calculated empathy, you’ve got everything you need to navigate the maze. Whether you’re a seller stepping away from your life’s work or a buyer stepping into a whole new one, this isn’t a transaction—it’s a turning point. So, use the LOI not as a formality, but as a strategic foundation. Be clear. Be kind. Be specific. Protect yourself—but don’t forget that generosity and clarity often go further than gamesmanship ever will. And finally, remember this: in small business M&A, momentum matters. But so does mindset. If you stay grounded in the big picture while managing the details with intention, you’ll not only close your deal—you’ll build something you’re proud of on the other side. You’ve got this. In the world of small business acquisitions, seller financing is often the bridge that gets the deal done. The buyer gets more time and flexibility to pay, the seller walks away with interest income—and in theory, everyone wins. But the deal doesn’t end when the wire goes through. Because what comes next—especially in the note documents—can make or break how that financing plays out. Enter the Confession of Judgment. This is one of those clauses that sounds legal and boring until it suddenly becomes very, very real. So let’s unpack what it is, when it’s used, and how to handle it if it shows up in your deal. What Is a Confession of Judgment? A Confession of Judgment (COJ) is exactly what it sounds like: it’s a written agreement—usually included in or attached to a promissory note—where one party (typically the buyer) agrees in advance that if they default on a payment, the other party (the seller) can immediately enter a court judgment without a trial or even advance notice. No hearing. No chance to explain. Just an immediate judgment entered against you, enforceable like any other legal debt. It’s a powerful tool—and one that’s controversial for exactly that reason. The Seller’s Perspective: Why a COJ Might Seem Reasonable Let’s give the seller their due here. In a seller-financed deal, especially when the seller is carrying a big portion of the purchase price over time, they’re stepping into a lender’s role—but without the institutional protections a traditional lender has. If the buyer defaults, the seller might be left: Holding an unsecured note Behind a bank on collateral priority With limited visibility into how the business is being run With no guarantees of recovery in the event of bankruptcy In that light, a COJ can feel like one of the few ways the seller has leverage.

It gives them a fast track to collect, keeps the buyer honest, and—perhaps most importantly—puts them ahead of the “nice guy creditor” line if things go sideways. So yes, it’s a serious ask. But it’s not always an unreasonable one. The Buyer’s Perspective: What’s the Risk? The risk, simply put, is disproportionate consequence. Here’s a real-world scenario: Let’s say you’ve paid $150,000 of a $300,000 seller note over the first two years. You miss one payment—maybe you’re dealing with a short-term cash flow squeeze or a payroll surprise. With a COJ in place, the seller can immediately file for judgment on the entire note balance, not just the amount you missed. Worse still: You might not get advance notice You don’t get a hearing It becomes part of your public record and affects your credit You now have to defend yourself after a judgment is entered So yes, it's enforceable. And yes, courts do uphold these agreements in certain states. But that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t negotiate terms around it—or at the very least, understand what you’re signing. When a COJ Might Be Worth Considering (With Caveats) If you’re a seller with legitimate concerns about repayment—and especially if: The buyer has limited operating history There are other lenders in the deal (like an SBA loan) The note is unsecured You’re subordinated to bank debt or equity investors ...then a well-structured COJ, with guardrails, might be something you ask for. But here’s the catch: it must be proportionate and conditional. And if you’re the buyer, here are smart ways to manage the risk without flat-out rejecting it: Balanced Approaches: How to Structure a Fair COJ (If You Must) Limit it to specific breaches. For example: “Only applicable if buyer misses two consecutive payments without cure.” Carve out cure periods. Give the buyer 10–15 business days to catch up before triggering the judgment rights. Credit for prior payments. The COJ should only apply to the unpaid balance—not the full face value of the original note. Notice and opportunity to resolve. Build in a process that lets the buyer resolve the issue before the seller takes it to court. State-by-state rules. Remember: some states prohibit COJs entirely or require strict procedural safeguards. Know your jurisdiction. Final Word: Leverage, Yes—But Keep It Proportional A confession of judgment isn’t evil. It’s a tool. And like most tools, it can be used responsibly—or it can cause a lot of damage if misused. If you’re a buyer, don’t sign one blindly. Ask questions. Negotiate clarity. Build in reasonable protections. If you’re a seller, be honest about why you want it. If the goal is to keep the buyer from ghosting? There are other ways—like UCC filings, milestone-based defaults, or partial guarantees. The best deals are built on fair risk, not fear.
